resources.string: Out of 200 million sperm, one reaches the egg in a Fallopian tube and fertilizes it. The outer layer of the egg hardens so that no other sperm can penetrate.

Out of 200 million sperm, one reaches the egg in a Fallopian tube and fertilizes it. This determines the genetic code of the embryo: eye color, sex, and traits—a unique human being emerges. Cell division begins and the first pregnancy hormones are produced.

The fertilized egg has divided multiple times into a tiny sphere that differentiates into the embryo and placenta. This cell cluster travels through the Fallopian tube to the uterus and implants into the uterine lining. Some women experience mild implantation bleeding during this process. As cell division continues, specialized cells begin forming organs, the nervous system, and the brain. The cardiovascular system, spine, connective and muscle tissues, and reproductive organs also start to develop.
By the end of this week, you may discover that you are pregnant. Your period will be missed, and hormone levels produced by the embryo are now high enough to be detected by a home pregnancy test.

The embryo is already about the size of a grain of rice. This week, the head, brain, blood cells, and blood vessels are forming. On an ultrasound, your baby looks like a small bright spot inside the amniotic sac. By the end of the 5th week, its tiny heart starts beating. The embryo is now connected to the placenta by a rudimentary umbilical cord. Pregnant women should completely stop alcohol and nicotine consumption, as the embryo is extremely sensitive. Hormonal changes may trigger early symptoms such as nausea, heightened sensitivity to smells, mood swings, fatigue, constipation, or bloating.

The embryo is now about 6 mm long and looks like a tiny bean. Small buds, which will become arms and legs, begin to emerge. This week, facial features begin to take shape, and vital organs like the liver, stomach, and intestines start growing. The spinal cord is present, and eye sockets and a mouth are visible. The fetus gently sways in the amniotic fluid. You may feel mild cramping similar to menstrual aches, caused by the stretching of uterine ligaments—this is completely normal.

The embryo grows rapidly now, about one millimeter each day. Its size is indicated in crown-rump length (CRL), the distance measured from head to buttocks. The digestive tract, heart, kidneys, brain, and lungs are in place and maturing. This is a crucial developmental stage; by the 10th week, all organ systems will be formed and will only need to mature.

The embryo measures 9 to 16 mm (CRL). The unborn child\'s heart beats at 140 to 150 beats per minute. The spine becomes mobile as vertebrae form around the spinal cord. Nerve cells are in a highly sensitive growth phase and are particularly vulnerable to harmful substances such as alcohol, nicotine, or unprescribed medications.

The embryo is now 17 to 24 mm (CRL). Arms, hands, legs, and feet are clearly visible. In male embryos, testicles begin to develop, though sex cannot yet be determined via ultrasound. However, an ultrasound will show clear baby movements, though it will take a few more weeks before you can feel them yourself. An ultrasound between the 9th and 12th week checks the heartbeat and embryonic movement. The expanding uterus may start pressing on your bladder.

The embryo measures 25 to 33 mm (CRL) and weighs under 4 g. Strong movements can be seen on ultrasound, and facial features are becoming clearer. The eyelids remain closed. Vital organs—liver, kidneys, intestines, brain, and lungs—are fully formed and functioning. The head accounts for about half of the total body length.

The risk of miscarriage decreases significantly after this week. Fluctuating hormone levels can cause noticeable mood swings, ranging from pure excitement to sudden tears. The face is fully formed with closed eyelids. The fetus is about 3 cm long and weighs around 15 g. Soft downy hair covers the skin. Your breasts may have grown, and your pants might start feeling tight. Your heart works harder to pump increased blood volume, which may cause fatigue or slight shortness of breath. Rest whenever needed.

The fetus is about 5 cm long and weighs around 16 g. The heart beats 120 to 160 times per minute. Muscles have developed so that elbows and wrists can flex. Spleen, liver, and bone marrow begin producing blood cells independently. By the end of the 12th week, morning sickness usually subsides for most women. Hormones soften pelvic ligaments, joints, and intervertebral discs to prepare your body for growth and birth.

The fetus weighs about 18 g, measures 6 cm (CRL), and has a head diameter of 21 mm. All organ systems have finished basic development and will now continue growing. Cartilage tissue is beginning to harden into bone. The baby can already move its lips, frown, and yawn. The placenta is now fully functional, supplying nutrients and oxygen while acting as a barrier against many harmful substances.

The fetal head diameter is 25 mm and weight is around 25 g. Genitals are developing clearly, and an ultrasound may sometimes reveal the sex. All organ systems are functional: the baby practices breathing movements in the amniotic fluid, though oxygen is supplied by the placenta. Touch, taste, balance, sucking, and grasping reflexes are all developing.

Head diameter is 28 to 37 mm, and weight reaches about 80 g. Your baby\'s hearing is now active, allowing it to hear sounds inside and outside the womb. Bone growth requires plenty of calcium. The heart is almost fully formed, and the liver and pancreas begin functioning. Be sure to drink enough water, as the risk of urinary tract infections increases.

Head diameter measures 32 to 40 mm, weight is about 90 g, and total length is around 9.4 cm. Organ formation is complete; the baby now focuses on gaining size and weight. Hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows begin to grow. If recommended by your doctor based on age or medical history, prenatal screening options such as amniocentesis may be discussed.

Head diameter is 35 to 44 mm, and weight is around 100 g. You may start feeling the first gentle flutterings of movement. The baby\'s sense of touch has developed enough to grasp the umbilical cord. The unborn child hears sounds such as your heartbeat, voice, or music. Ultrasound accuracy for determining the baby\'s sex is now very high.

Head diameter is 38 to 48 mm, weight is about 125 g, and length is around 12 cm. Fetal movements are now distinct, with clear rest and active phases. Movements are often felt most when you relax in the evening. Leg cramps or varicose veins may occur due to pressure on pelvic blood vessels. The uterus has grown significantly, reaching almost to the navel. A dark line (linea nigra) may appear on your abdomen.

Head diameter is 42 to 51 mm, and weight is about 200 g. The expanding uterus provides plenty of room for movement. The baby\'s eyes move back and forth behind closed eyelids. Now is a great time to research birth options and sign up for childbirth preparation classes, which typically start around week 20.

Head diameter is 46 to 55 mm, weight is about 300 g. Growth rate slows slightly as small fat deposits form to help with body temperature regulation after birth. The baby swallows amniotic fluid and excretes it through the urinary tract, training the kidneys and swallowing reflexes. Fetal movements are now easily felt by the mother.

Head diameter is 50 to 58 mm, weight is about 350 g. The baby gains weight rapidly. The inner ear balance organ is fully developed, giving the baby spatial awareness. Fine downy hair (lanugo) and a protective waxy layer (vernix caseosa) cover the skin. You may feel painless uterine tightenings (Braxton Hicks contractions) as your body prepares for birth.

Head diameter is 52 to 62 mm, weight is about 500 g. The baby develops a regular sleep-wake cycle and becomes more aware of its environment. If you feel rhythmic twitches in your abdomen, the baby simply has hiccups! Pelvic floor exercises help support the extra weight. Stretch marks may appear as the skin stretches.

Head diameter is 58 to 69 mm, weight is about 580 g. Amniotic fluid volume increases. The baby responds to external sounds with specific movements. Your doctor will monitor your hemoglobin levels to ensure proper oxygen transport to the baby.

Head diameter is 61 to 72 mm, weight is about 700 g. The baby\'s sense of taste is well developed. It reacts to bright light or loud noise with vigorous movement and an increased pulse. Fat deposits under the skin make it smoother and less wrinkled.

Head diameter is 64 to 75 mm, weight is about 800 g. As the baby grows, space in the uterus becomes more restricted. Lungs continue maturing. Sleeping at night can become challenging due to belly size and active nighttime baby movements.

Head diameter is 66 to 77 mm, weight is about 900 g. The baby\'s eyes open. A light source directed at the abdomen can prompt a response with movement and faster heart rate. Babies born prematurely from week 26 onward have an increasingly good chance of survival with specialized medical care.

Head diameter is 70 to 80 mm, weight is about 1,000 g. Lung maturity reaches a major milestone. Iron supplements may be recommended if blood hemoglobin is low. Common late-pregnancy symptoms like heartburn, back pain, shortness of breath, or frequent urination may occur as the baby takes up more room.
Head diameter is 72 to 83 mm, weight is about 1,100 g. Many babies turn into a head-down birthing position. Fluid retention (edema) in ankles and feet is common—elevate your legs whenever possible.

Head diameter is 74 to 86 mm, weight is about 1,250 g. From week 30, prenatal checkups will occur more frequently. Your doctor will check fetal growth, position, and heartbeat as anticipation builds for delivery day.

Head diameter is 76 to 88 mm, weight is about 1,400 g. The fetus grows rapidly in size and weight. Braxton Hicks contractions become more frequent. Small amounts of nutrient-rich first milk (colostrum) may leak from your breasts.

Head diameter is 78 to 90 mm, weight is about 1,600 g. The baby gains 150 to 200 g per week. Movements slow down into rolling or stretching motions as space decreases. Most babies are settled head-down. Make sure all essential baby items are ready.

Head diameter is 80 to 93 mm, weight is about 1,800 g, and total length is 41 to 43 cm. Lightening contractions help the baby\'s head settle deeper into the pelvis. Fat reserves continue to accumulate to help regulate body temperature after birth.

Head diameter is 82 to 95 mm, weight is about 2,000 g. Calcium demand is high as bones harden. Pack your hospital bag and finalize home preparations. Contact your doctor immediately if you notice leaking amniotic fluid.

Head diameter is 84 to 97 mm, weight is about 2,250 g. Lightening contractions position the baby deeper in the pelvis, easing pressure on your lungs and stomach. Rest frequently as your body carries the extra weight.

Head diameter is 86 to 99 mm, weight is about 2,550 g. Signs of approaching delivery include passing of the mucus plug, water breaking, or regular labor contractions. Inform your doctor or midwife when these signs occur.

Head diameter is 87 to 101 mm, weight is about 2,750 g. Fingernails and toenails are fully formed, and head hair may reach up to 5 cm in length. Your body prepares for nursing and birth, with blood flow through the placenta reaching about 80 liters daily.

Head diameter is 89 to 102 mm, weight is about 2,950 g. The baby is considered full-term from week 37. Cranial sutures remain soft and flexible to allow the head to adapt during passage through the birth canal.
Head diameter is 90 to 103 mm, weight is about 3,100 g. Space in the womb is very tight, so movements are limited. The baby\'s eyes are open when awake, ready for life outside.

Head diameter is 91 to 104 mm, weight is about 3,250 g, and length is about 50 cm. You may feel a sudden nesting instinct with energy to clean and organize. Be sure to get plenty of rest to save your strength for labor.

About 10% of pregnancies continue past the estimated due date. Your doctor will monitor placental function, oxygen supply, and fluid levels closely. Labor may be induced if recommended to prevent post-term risks. Your baby will be here soon!
About 10% of pregnancies reach week 41. Frequent checkups ensure the placenta continues providing sufficient oxygen and nutrients. Medical induction of labor may be discussed with your doctor.
At 42 weeks, medical induction of labor is routine to ensure a safe birth. Your waiting is almost over, and you will soon welcome your newborn!
Information for this week is not yet available.
